title: Noctilucent clouds
hook: The highest clouds on Earth glow electric blue in the middle of a summer night.
peek: About 80 kilometres up, far above the weather, wisps of ice catch sunlight long after sunset and shine blue against a dark sky. Nobody reported them until 1885, and they seem to be showing up more often than they used to.
lede: Ordinary clouds sit within the lowest dozen kilometres of the sky. Noctilucent, or night-shining, clouds float about 80 kilometres up, in the mesosphere, the coldest layer of the atmosphere. They are so high that they stay lit by the Sun after the ground below has gone dark, glowing pale blue and silver on summer nights.

bullets.text: There are no clear reports of them before 1885, two years after the eruption of Krakatoa filled the sky with ash and made people watch twilight closely. The German astronomer Otto Jesse studied them and gave them their name.
They are made of tiny ice crystals. Water vapour is scarce that high, so the ice needs something to grow on, and the best candidate is fine dust left by meteors burning up in the atmosphere.

They are best seen at latitudes roughly between 50 and 70 degrees, in the weeks around midsummer, when the Sun is well below the horizon but still lighting the upper sky. Look low towards the north after sunset.

In 2007 NASA launched a satellite called AIM to study them from above. Observers have found the clouds appearing more often, brighter and farther from the poles than in the past, and rocket exhaust can even seed new ones.
